description: A conical hat of dried palm leaves stitched over bamboo rings, with a cloth chin strap.  Its wide brim keeps the sun out of your eyes and the rain off your face, but it will not keep the rest of you dry.
A thin plastic motorbike half-helmet with a snap chin strap, the kind sold on every street corner after the helmet law was first discussed.  It is more for the traffic police than for your skull.
An áo mưa cánh dơi: a huge sheet of thin plastic with a hood and sleeves, cut wide enough to drape over you and the motorbike handlebars.  It keeps the monsoon off, and it is stifling.
Cheap molded foam sandals, white or blue, perforated with a honeycomb of holes.  Worn by everyone from grandmothers to construction workers.  They dry in minutes and protect you from almost nothing.
A loose, collarless southern shirt of thin cotton with two front pockets.  Cool in the heat and quick to dry.
Long cotton sleeves with thumb loops, worn by motorbike riders to keep the sun off their arms.  In a city without air conditioning, anything that blocks the sun is worth wearing.
A heavy, square-tipped chopping blade with a wooden handle, used to split coconuts, clear brush and hack bamboo.  Every rural household owns one, and many city ones do too.
A suitcase-sized single-burner stove that runs on a slim butane canister slotted into its side.  Street vendors cook everything on these, from phở broth to grilled pork.
A thùng xốp: a big white polystyrene box with a lid, used by market vendors to keep fish and ice.  The thick foam walls slow down how fast its contents warm up in the heat.
